To the Semi-Centennial Convention with the Theta Chapter, 1883
Sing for my sake the old refrain:
Then till the sands of life are run,
We'll sing to thee Psi Upsilon,
Long live Psi Upsilon! Psi Upsilon!
-Chester A. Arthur, Theta 1848
At the Convention of 1929, with the Eta, held in Washington
Twenty-seven chapters! That combines a force that rightly directed will mean much
for the progress of our country. They represent the character of men that we need; men
who are intellectual, who are strong, who are loyal, who have high ideals and have
courage, have comradeship and are for the public and the country all the time, without
talking about it. That last is exceptional. I am glad and proud to belong to it.
-William H. Taft, Beta 1878

FOREWORD
By Scott Turner, Phi '02
President, Executive Council of Psi Upsilon
IN 1884, 'IHE STORY of the first fifty
years of Psi Upsilon was written by
an able historian, and published as
the Epitome. The edition was not
large, and long ago it became a rare
volume; now, the book is considered
a collector's item.
The Fraternity continued its triumphal march for another half century. Year by year history was made;
familiar faces disappeared and fresh
ones took their places; additional
Chapters were chartered, and the
old ones established new records of
achievement; original chapter halls
were replaced by residential chapter
houses; conventions met, legislated,
and adjourned only to convene again
the following year; social gatherings
of notable importance were held; interesting and significant events transpired and were duly recorded; essen49
tial data and priceless memorabilia
were stowed away for future reference.
Thus, by 1933, when Psi Upsilon
celebrated its one-hundredth anniversary, a wealth of material had accumulated, awaiting the loving care
of another historiographer who was
willing to devote the time and labor
necessary to make the story available
to all members of our Fraternity.
Unfortunately, the chronicles of
those years of activity were not always as complete as they should have
been; many documents remained in
the possession of Chapters, or of individuals, and were not sent to headquarters; those that were delivered
to New York were stored in an inconvenient place, and remained in
part unclassified and uncatalogued,
so that reference to them was exceedingly difficult. The next step in
preparing a history of Psi Upsilon
was obviously to make the archives
more accessible. This was done in
1939, through the fine efforts of our
Archivist, working under the authority of the Executive Council. At last,
the records and memorabilia were
assembled and installed for convenient use, in a room specially equipped
for the purpose at Fraternity headquarters.
The mailing lists, as always, were
far from current, and the manual
method of recording changes of addresses had become obsolete. The
